source.title: Long-Range Distillation: Distilling 10,000 Years of Simulated Climate into Long Timestep AI Weather Models
source.authors: Scott A. Martin; Noah D. Brenowitz; Dale R. Durran; Michael S. Pritchard

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study varies synthetic training-data volume for weather forecasting and explicitly reports that forecast skill does not follow a power law with dataset size, refining or challenging the proposed transfer of power-law scaling to other settings.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Kaplan et al. for motivation, but reports no new language-model scaling results. Only its own synthetic-data scaling results are included; other forecast comparisons do not test the claim versions.
record.test_reason: In a new setting (a diffusion weather-forecast student trained on synthetic climate data), the study varies training-data volume over about 2.5 orders of magnitude. It reports validation loss and CRPS, and states that CRPS does not follow a power law in dataset size. Model capacity is fixed throughout, and the authors name this as a possible bottleneck. So it is a new-setting result bearing on V5, not a clean refutation (T5).
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude S2S skill improves with synthetic data volume, with diminishing returns rather than a power law, at fixed model capacity. They attribute this either to saturating the teacher climate's variability or to a capacity bottleneck, and propose joint model/data scaling as future work.
record.recipe_differences: This is a weather-forecasting synthetic-data scaling experiment, not a language-model pretraining scaling-law fit; student architecture is held fixed while training-data volume changes.
record.method_sensitivity: Training-data volume and sampling diversity change validation loss and forecast outcomes; model capacity is fixed.

fits_no_version.finding: At equal sample count (40 years), samples drawn randomly from the 11,000-year simulation beat 100 contiguous years. Gains come largely from sample diversity rather than sample count.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Effective data scaling depends on sample diversity/independence, not just nominal dataset size.

fits_no_version.finding: A linear inverse model's validation MSE and NLL improve steadily with synthetic training years up to about 1,000 years (Fig. 10). This is a non-neural model, and no functional form is stated.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Data-volume gains for classical statistical estimators fitted on synthetic data.

record.code_released: The authors state that code will be released in a public GitHub repository upon publication; URL not stated.
record.peer_reviewed: preprint; manuscript submitted to Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems (JAMES)
record.problems: The scaling experiment holds architecture capacity fixed, and the authors state that CRPS does not follow a power law. The text gives no uncertainty estimate for the reported 14% CRPS reduction.
record.rows_left_out: No other results were omitted that directly test the claim versions.

untested.parts: Joint scaling of model size and data, or compute scaling, in this domain; an explicit fitted functional form for loss versus data; image, video, repeated-data and fine-tuning scaling laws.
Not tested: no language-model pretraining loss.
Not tested: no extrapolation from fits.
Not tested: no LM downstream tasks.
Not tested: no comparison of fitting choices.

missing.what: Intermediate dataset sizes (e.g. 100 and 1,000 years) for minimum validation loss and CRPS. These are needed to judge the curve's shape; values appear only in a figure.
LIM validation MSE/NLL versus synthetic training years, improving up to about 1,000 years.
Informal observation: a quantile-regression student trained on 11,000 years learned weakly and showed no data-scaling benefit. Whether data scaling appears depends on the training objective.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'challenges' label is too strong. V5 inherits V1's condition that the other factors are not the bottleneck, and capacity is held fixed here, which the authors themselves name as a likely cause. No uncertainty is given for the scaling results. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test held-out pretraining loss scaling in language models with parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run power-law fits are used to predict much larger runs.
No fixed-compute parameter/token allocation is tested.
The study does not compare architecture shapes at fixed parameter count.

Tests synthetic-data-volume scaling for weather forecast models at fixed student architecture; does not test other modalities or repeated-data, fine-tuning, and transfer scaling laws as systematic scaling curves.
The study evaluates weather forecast skill, not downstream language-model task performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss.
It does not estimate language-model scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocations under alternative fitting choices.

rows.subject: Distilled S2S student model (40-year contiguous DLESyM training data)
rows.operation_detail: Trained the S2S student using a 40-year contiguous synthetic dataset and evaluated training and validation EDM denoising loss.
rows.measure: Training and validation EDM denoising loss
rows.value: Overfitting appears once trained beyond ∼1M samples, corresponding to ∼15,000 training steps.
rows.note: The loss outcome is reported explicitly, but this is not evidence of a power-law curve.
rows.check: A single 40-year training curve showing overfitting after about 1M samples. It is a training-dynamics observation, not a scaling relation; it only matters as the small end of the r2/r3 comparison.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3.2.1, Figure 5a; Appendix B, Table B2.

rows.subject: Distilled S2S student model (11,000-year DLESyM training data)
rows.operation_detail: Trained the S2S student on the full synthetic dataset and evaluated training and validation EDM denoising loss.
rows.measure: Training and validation EDM denoising loss
rows.value: No signs of overfitting; training and validation losses match closely. Minimum validation loss improves as training years increase.
rows.note: The paper reports improvement with more data, but does not report a power-law relationship.
rows.check: Minimum validation EDM loss improves steadily as training years grow by orders of magnitude (Fig. 5b, log axes). The text never states whether this follows a power law, and capacity is fixed. Direction matches V5; the functional form cannot be read from the text. The row's two parts (no overfitting at 11k years, loss scaling) should be separated.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3.2.1, paragraph comparing 40-year and 11,000-year training; Figure 5a–b; Table B2.

rows.subject: Distilled S2S student model
rows.operation_detail: Compared forecast skill as the synthetic training dataset increased from 40 years to 11,000 years.

conditions.value: Global mean 2 m temperature CRPS at 4-week lead time

rows.baseline: Training on 40 years of DLESyM simulation
rows.value: Training on 11,000 years yields a 14% reduction in CRPS compared to training on 40 years.
rows.note: The paper says CRPS does not follow a power law with dataset size; it suggests diminishing returns or fixed model capacity as possible explanations.
rows.check: CRPS falls 14% from 40 to 11,000 years, but the authors say it does not follow a power law and is weaker than LM scaling. This is at fixed 149M capacity, which may be the bottleneck the version excludes. CRPS is a downstream skill metric rather than the training loss.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3.2.1, Figure 5b: 14% reduction in week-4 2 m temperature CRPS from 40 to 11,000 training years.

rows.subject: Distilled S2S student model (40-year randomly sampled DLESyM data)
rows.operation_detail: Trained on 40 years of samples randomly drawn from across the 11,000-year simulation and compared validation EDM loss with contiguous-data training.
rows.baseline: 40 years sampled as a contiguous block
rows.value: The randomly sampled model outperforms training on 100 years of contiguous data, while lagging the 1,000-year and 11,000-year models.
rows.note: The randomly sampled model eventually overfits, but remains regularized longer than the contiguous 40-year model. This suggests sample diversity affects the result, rather than establishing a power law.
rows.check: Compares random versus contiguous sampling at equal sample count (data diversity). It does not measure a scaling curve. Belongs under fits_no_version.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3.2.1, random-versus-contiguous sampling paragraph; Figure 6a–b; Table B2.

relationships.condition: Diffusion weather student (149M, fixed capacity) trained on 40–11,000 years of synthetic DLESyM data, S2S week-4 T2m
relationships.reason: Validation loss falls steadily with data (r2), but week-4 CRPS gains only 14% and the authors say it does not follow a power law (r3). They attribute this to a fixed-capacity bottleneck or saturated teacher diversity, so power-law form is not shown in this regime.
relationships.display_finding: Validation loss decreased steadily, but week-4 CRPS improved only 14% and did not follow a power law, possibly because of fixed capacity or saturated teacher diversity.

relation.reason: The study varies synthetic training-data volume and directly evaluates validation loss and forecast CRPS, explicitly assessing whether CRPS follows a power law.

tranche.reason: Although weather forecasting is a new setting, the explicit finding that CRPS does not follow a power law qualifies V5. T5 captures this result requiring the version to be qualified.

source_check.notes: The scaling sweep evaluates withheld DLESyM simulations. No power-law fit for EDM validation loss is reported; teacher-diversity saturation and student-capacity bottlenecks are proposed explanations, not established causes.
